summary: How to organize the code inside one deployable part, so that business rules stay free of technical details.

blocks.title: Select a structure for one code base

items.when: Simple data in, data out, few rules
Real business rules that will live for years
Many features that are mostly independent
items.use: Vertical slices, alone or inside a hexagonal core

items.when: Complex rules about what is valid
Reads and writes have very different needs
items.use: CQRS, at the lowest level that works

items.when: History is the product, as in a ledger
items.use: Event sourcing, in that one part only

items.when: Two things must be consistent at each moment
A short delay between two things is acceptable
items.use: Two aggregates and a domain event

items.when: The only need is a stream of changes for other services
items.use: An outbox or CDC, not event sourcing

items.when: The only need is an audit trail

items.text: Business rules must not depend on technical details.
Code in the core imports nothing from an adapter, a framework, or a database library.
Check the direction of dependencies automatically, with an architecture test or a lint rule.
Keep one composition root at the edge. It creates and connects parts, and decides nothing.
Make each dependency an interface (a port), not a concrete class. Then a test can replace it.
Share code between slices when it must change together, not because it looks similar.
One transaction changes one aggregate. One aggregate refers to another only by its ID.
Use value objects freely. They are the cheapest and most useful domain model pattern.
Make a remote call outside the transaction. Record the state before and after the call.
Always map between the core and the public API, and between the core and published messages.
"Hexagonal or microservices?" They are not alternatives. They are two different levels.
A port that copies the technology, such as `SqlOrderPort.executeQuery`. A port speaks the language of the business.
Business rules in adapters, such as a controller that decides if an order is valid.
Framework annotations in the domain model. The core then depends on the framework.
An aggregate that is too large, such as a customer that contains all its orders.
A test full of mocks. It breaks when you refactor, also when the behavior is correct.
Two vocabularies, such as onion and clean, mixed in one code base.
CQRS or event sourcing as the default, or because "it scales" with no number.
Entity services: one service for each table, with create, read, update, delete. They hide no decision.
An anemic domain model: domain names, only getters and setters, and all rules in services.

blocks.title: Test doubles
rows: Returns fixed answers, with no logic
Expects some calls, and fails if they differ
A stub that also records the calls for the test

items.text: Complexity is anything that makes a system hard to understand or change. It is not size.
A deep module has a simple interface and a lot of functionality behind it.
The interface is the cost to each caller. The implementation is the benefit.
A small unit is good only when it hides something. Many tiny classes add interfaces.
Put code that shares knowledge in one module, not one module for each step in time.
A pass-through method or gateway only forwards calls. It adds an interface and hides nothing.
Pull complexity down. A simple interface is more important than a simple implementation.
Define errors out of existence, but never hide an error that the caller must know.
Design each important module twice, with very different approaches. Then compare them.
Write the interface comment first. A long, hard comment shows an interface that is too complex.

blocks.title: Three symptoms of complexity
rows: A small change needs edits in many places
You must know a lot to change code safely
Not clear what to change. Found in production. The worst one
A dependency that nobody can see
